name: Camera Angle Studio
description: One photo of a model, six camera angles (fisheye, bird's eye, low angle, Dutch angle, macro, worm's eye), two ways — straight from a tile, and through an AI director who reads the photo and decides what each angle should show — one row above the other to compare.
markdownDescription:
## Camera Angle Studio

One photo of a model, six camera angles, two ways of asking for them — one row above the other, so you can compare.

1. **Reference photo** — any clear photo of a person. The face, the clothes and the place stay; only the camera moves.
2. **Six angle tiles** — fisheye, bird's eye, low angle, Dutch angle, macro, worm's eye. One tile per angle, no writing.
3. **Row 1, from the tile** — each tile goes straight into an image. Fast, cheap, good for most jobs.
4. **Row 2, with a director** — the same tile goes to an AI director who reads the photo and decides what the angle should reveal, then writes the prompt. Worth it when the angle has to say something.
5. Same photo, same six angles, two answers each. Pick the way that fits the job; delete the row you do not need.

data.label: How it works
data.title: Camera angle studio — how it works

data.text: One clear photo of a person: the face visible, the clothes readable, the place recognisable. Every image below gets it as a reference and keeps all three. Replace it with your own photo, or with a model card from Model Creator Studio — this one is.
data.label: Step 1
data.title: 1 · Reference photo

data.text: Top row: one picker per angle — a Lens tile for the fisheye, a Framing tile for the rest. Each tile goes straight into the image under it with no prompt writing: the tile already carries the photographer's words for that angle. Swap a tile for any other angle or shot size and rerun that column alone.
data.label: Step 2
data.title: 2 · Six angles from tiles

data.text: The same tiles again, but each first goes to an AI director who looks at the photo and decides what the angle should show — the eyes in the fisheye, the shoes in the worm's eye, the fabric in the macro — and writes where the camera stands in plain physical words. Its paragraph becomes the prompt of the image under it. Open a director to read what it decided; compare its image with the tile-only image above.
data.label: Step 3
data.title: 3 · The same six angles with a director

data.label: Tile · Fisheye
data.prompt: The model from the reference photo photographed again from a new camera position: {Fisheye || a different camera angle}. Keep the person, the clothes and the place exactly as in the reference photo — same face, same hair, same outfit, same background and light; only the camera changes. Photorealistic, natural colours matching the photo, no text, no watermark.

data.label: Director · Fisheye
data.userInput: Camera angle: {Fisheye || a different camera angle}. Write the prompt.
data.systemPrompt: You are a fashion photography director. You get one photo of a model and one camera angle. Look at the photo first: the clothes, the pose, the most striking element (a collar, a shoe, the hair, the eyes), the surroundings, the direction and warmth of the light. Then decide what THIS angle should show — a real photographer does not just tilt the camera, they choose what the angle reveals. Write ONE paragraph of three to five sentences that is the complete image prompt: exactly where the camera stands and where it points, in plain physical words (at floor level thirty centimetres from the shoes, tilted up along the body); what becomes big and what recedes; how the surroundings frame the person from there; the light and the colours matching the photo. Always say the model from the reference photo. No lens jargon, no composition rules, no headers, no quotation marks. Output only the paragraph.
